title: textkit: text normalization and formatting utilities
description: textkit collects the small text helpers used across the content platform: whitespace and token normalization, identifier case conversion, slugs, previews, word wrapping and justification for plain-text newsletters, sentence splitting and readability scoring. It also provides typo-tolerant matching for search suggestions and tag pickers, a lightweight template renderer for notification emails, a CSV line splitter for bulk imports, and Markdown heading/TOC utilities. Pure standard-library Python, no I/O.

functions.signature: def normalize_whitespace(text: str) -> str:
functions.summary: Collapse whitespace runs into single spaces and trim the ends
functions.spec:
Collapse every run of whitespace in `text` into a single ASCII space and
strip leading and trailing whitespace.

"Whitespace" means any character for which str.isspace() is true: spaces, tabs,
newlines, non-breaking spaces (U+00A0), em spaces and so on. This is the first
cleanup step applied to titles, excerpts and user-submitted copy.

Examples:
    normalize_whitespace("  Hello \t\n world  ") == "Hello world"
    normalize_whitespace("") == ""
functions.clarification:
Invisible zero-width characters that come in with text pasted from rich-text
editors must be deleted outright: U+200B (zero width space), U+200C, U+200D,
U+2060 (word joiner) and U+FEFF (byte order mark). They are not treated as
whitespace (no space is inserted where they were), so "co​op" becomes
"coop" and "﻿Title" becomes "Title".

functions.signature: def tokenize_words(text: str) -> List[str]:
functions.summary: Split text into lowercase word tokens
functions.spec:
Split `text` into lowercase word tokens, in order of appearance.

Tokens are made of letters and digits; matching is Unicode-aware, so accented
words such as "café" or "naïve" are single tokens. Whitespace and
punctuation (including underscores and hyphens) separate tokens and are
discarded. Returns an empty list when the text contains no letters or digits.

Examples:
    tokenize_words("Hello, World! 42 times") == ["hello", "world", "42", "times"]
    tokenize_words("state-of-the-art") == ["state", "of", "the", "art"]
functions.clarification:
Apostrophes inside words are kept: an apostrophe (ASCII ' or the typographic
U+2019) that sits directly between two letters stays part of the token, and
U+2019 is normalized to ASCII "'". So "Don’t" -> "don't" and "it's" -> "it's".
Apostrophes anywhere else (quotes like 'this', or plural possessives such as
"users'") still act as separators.

functions.signature: def split_identifier(name: str) -> List[str]:
functions.summary: Split an identifier in any naming convention into lowercase words
functions.spec:
Split an identifier written in any common naming convention into its
lowercase component words.

Accepted conventions: snake_case, SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE, kebab-case,
dot.separated, camelCase, PascalCase and space separated words (mixed forms are
fine). Rules:
  * "_", "-", "." and whitespace are separators; empty parts are dropped.
  * A new word starts where a lowercase letter or a digit is followed by an
    uppercase letter ("userName" -> "user", "name").
  * Digits stay attached to the letters before them ("utf8Decoder" -> "utf8", "decoder").
  * Returned words are lowercase. An identifier without letters or digits gives [].

Examples:
    split_identifier("userAccount_id") == ["user", "account", "id"]
    split_identifier("MAX_RETRY-count") == ["max", "retry", "count"]
functions.clarification:
Runs of capital letters are acronyms and stay together as one word, except that
when an uppercase run is followed by a lowercase letter, the last capital of the
run starts the next word: "parseHTTPResponse" -> ["parse", "http", "response"],
"XMLParser" -> ["xml", "parser"], "getURL" -> ["get", "url"].

functions.signature: def to_snake_case(name: str) -> str:
functions.summary: Convert an identifier to snake_case
functions.spec:
Convert an identifier written in any naming convention to snake_case.

The words are obtained with split_identifier() and joined with "_" (so the
result is all lowercase). Returns "" when the input has no words.

Examples:
    to_snake_case("userAccountId") == "user_account_id"
    to_snake_case("Content-Type") == "content_type"
functions.clarification:
Leading underscores mark private or internal names and must be preserved
exactly as they appear: "_cachedValue" -> "_cached_value", "__InitHook" ->
"__init_hook". Trailing underscores are not preserved ("trailing_" -> "trailing").

functions.signature: def to_camel_case(name: str, upper_first: bool = False) -> str:
functions.summary: Convert an identifier to camelCase or PascalCase
functions.spec:
Convert an identifier written in any naming convention to camelCase, or to
PascalCase when `upper_first` is True.

The words come from split_identifier(). The first word stays lowercase
(capitalized when upper_first=True); every following word is capitalized
(first character upper case, the rest lower case). Words are concatenated
without separators. Returns "" when there are no words.

Examples:
    to_camel_case("user_account_id") == "userAccountId"
    to_camel_case("user_account_id", upper_first=True) == "UserAccountId"
functions.clarification:
The output is used as a generated JSON/JavaScript field name, so it must be a
valid identifier: if the result would start with a digit, prefix it with a
single underscore. "3d_model" -> "_3dModel", and with upper_first=True
"2fa-enabled" -> "_2faEnabled".

functions.signature: def humanize_identifier(name: str) -> str:
functions.summary: Turn a field identifier into a readable label for admin screens
functions.spec:
Turn a field or column identifier into a human-readable label for admin
screens and CSV headers.

The words come from split_identifier(). The label is the words joined by single
spaces, with the first word capitalized and the remaining words lowercase.
Words in the acronym set {"api", "id", "url", "html", "http", "json", "sql",
"uuid"} are written fully uppercase wherever they appear. Returns "" for an
identifier without words.

Examples:
    humanize_identifier("createdAt") == "Created at"
    humanize_identifier("api_key") == "API key"
functions.clarification:
Foreign-key columns get a shorter label: when the identifier has more than one
word and its last word is "id", that last word is dropped ("author_id" ->
"Author", "parentPostId" -> "Parent post"). A lone "id" still becomes "ID", and
"id" in any other position is kept ("id_card" -> "ID card").

functions.signature: def edit_distance(a: str, b: str) -> int:
functions.summary: Compute the typo-tolerant edit distance between two strings
functions.spec:
Return the edit distance between `a` and `b`: the minimum number of
single-character edits needed to turn `a` into `b`.

Inserting, deleting or substituting one character each cost 1. The comparison
is case-sensitive, and the distance is symmetric:
edit_distance(a, b) == edit_distance(b, a). Used by search suggestions for
typo tolerance.

Examples:
    edit_distance("kitten", "sitting") == 3
    edit_distance("", "abc") == 3
functions.clarification:
Swapped neighbours are the most common typo and must count as one edit:
transposing two adjacent characters costs 1 (the "optimal string alignment"
variant, where no substring is edited more than once).
edit_distance("teh", "the") == 1 and edit_distance("recieve", "receive") == 1.

functions.signature: def similarity(a: str, b: str) -> float:
functions.summary: Score how similar two strings are on a 0-1 scale
functions.spec:
Return a similarity score between 0.0 and 1.0 for two strings, based on
edit_distance():

    score = 1 - edit_distance(a, b) / max(len(a), len(b))

rounded to 2 decimal places with round(). Two empty strings score 1.0.

Examples:
    similarity("kitten", "sitting") == 0.57
    similarity("abc", "abc") == 1.0
functions.clarification:
Scores are case-insensitive: both strings are casefolded (str.casefold())
before the distance and the lengths are computed, so
similarity("Python", "python") == 1.0 and similarity("Graph", "graphs") == 0.83.

functions.signature: def rank_matches(query: str, candidates: Sequence[str], limit: int = 5, min_score: float = 0.0) -> List[Tuple[str, float]]:
functions.summary: Rank candidate strings by similarity to a query
functions.spec:
Rank `candidates` by how closely they match `query` and return the best ones
as (candidate, score) pairs, best score first. Used by the tag picker.

The score of a candidate is similarity(query, candidate). Candidates scoring
below `min_score` are dropped, then at most `limit` pairs are returned.
Duplicate candidate strings are only ranked once. `candidates` is not modified.
Raises ValueError if limit < 0.

Example:
    rank_matches("python", ["java", "python", "pythons"], limit=2)
        == [("python", 1.0), ("pythons", 0.86)]
functions.clarification:
Candidates with equal scores keep the order in which they were supplied
(editors list preferred tags first); ties must not be re-sorted alphabetically
or by length. For example rank_matches("cat", ["hat", "bat", "cut", "cat"])
starts with ("cat", 1.0), ("hat", 0.67), ("bat", 0.67), ("cut", 0.67).

functions.signature: def closest_match(word: str, vocabulary: Iterable[str], max_distance: int = 2) -> Optional[str]:
functions.summary: Suggest the closest vocabulary entry for a misspelled word
functions.spec:
Suggest the vocabulary entry closest to `word` (the "did you mean ...?" hint
under the search box).

Distances are computed with edit_distance() on the lowercased strings. Returns
the entry with the smallest distance, provided that distance is <=
max_distance; returns None when nothing is close enough or the vocabulary is
empty. When several entries share the smallest distance, the one that appears
first in `vocabulary` wins. The entry is returned with its original spelling.
Raises ValueError if max_distance is negative.

Examples:
    closest_match("pyhton", ["python", "pandas"]) == "python"
    closest_match("zzz", ["python"]) is None
functions.clarification:
Short words get less slack: when `word` has 4 characters or fewer, at most 1
edit is allowed no matter how large max_distance is (with 2 edits nearly every
3-letter query would match something). The cap only ever lowers the limit, so
max_distance=0 still means exact (case-insensitive) matches only.

functions.signature: def slugify(text: str, max_length: Optional[int] = None) -> str:
functions.summary: Build an ASCII URL slug from a title
functions.spec:
Build a URL slug from a title.

The text is split into words with tokenize_words(). Each word is reduced to
ASCII by stripping diacritics (Unicode NFKD decomposition, then dropping
non-ASCII characters), after which any remaining character other than a-z and
0-9 is removed; words that end up empty are discarded. The remaining words are
joined with "-", so the slug only contains a-z, 0-9 and "-".

If `max_length` is given, the slug is shortened to at most max_length
characters and never ends with "-". Raises ValueError if max_length is given
and is < 1.

Examples:
    slugify("Hello, World!") == "hello-world"
    slugify("Crème Brûlée Recipes") == "creme-brulee-recipes"
    slugify("50% off: Summer Sale") == "50-off-summer-sale"
functions.clarification:
Shortening must not cut a word in half: keep as many whole words as fit within
max_length. Only when the first word alone is longer than max_length is that
word cut to max_length characters. So slugify("The quick brown fox",
max_length=12) == "the-quick", not "the-quick-br".

functions.signature: def truncate_text(text: str, max_chars: int, ellipsis: str = "...") -> str:
functions.summary: Truncate text for previews on a word boundary with an ellipsis
functions.spec:
Shorten `text` for previews and teasers without cutting words in half.

The text is first cleaned with normalize_whitespace(). If the cleaned text has
at most `max_chars` characters it is returned as is. Otherwise the result is the
longest run of whole leading words (joined by single spaces) such that the
words plus `ellipsis` fit in max_chars characters, followed by `ellipsis`. If
not even the first word fits, the first word is hard-cut so that the result is
exactly max_chars characters long. Raises ValueError if
max_chars <= len(ellipsis).

Examples:
    truncate_text("The quick brown fox jumps", 15) == "The quick..."
    truncate_text("Short text", 50) == "Short text"
functions.clarification:
Punctuation left dangling at the cut point is removed before the ellipsis is
added: strip any trailing characters from , ; : . ! ? - off the kept words.
"Hello, world and everyone" cut after "Hello," gives "Hello..." rather than
"Hello,...". The stripping happens after the cut is chosen; it never lets more
words in.

functions.signature: def wrap_text(text: str, width: int) -> List[str]:
functions.summary: Greedy word-wrap text to a column width
functions.spec:
Greedy word-wrap `text` into lines of at most `width` characters (used for
plain-text emails).

The text is cleaned with normalize_whitespace() and split into words on spaces.
Words are added to the current line, separated by single spaces, as long as the
line stays within `width`; otherwise a new line is started with that word. Lines
have no leading or trailing spaces. Empty or whitespace-only text gives [].
Raises ValueError if width < 1.

Example:
    wrap_text("the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog", 10)
        == ["the quick", "brown fox", "jumps over", "the lazy", "dog"]
functions.clarification:
Words are never broken: a word longer than `width` (URLs, product codes) goes
on a line of its own even though that line is longer than width, and hyphens
are not break points ("well-known" stays one word, on one line).

functions.signature: def justify_text(text: str, width: int) -> List[str]:
functions.summary: Fully justify text to a fixed column width
functions.spec:
Fully justify `text` to a fixed column width for plain-text newsletters.

Lines are produced with wrap_text(text, width). Every line except the last one
is then stretched to exactly `width` characters by widening the gaps between
its words: the extra spaces are spread as evenly as possible, and when they do
not divide evenly the leftmost gaps get one more space than the others.
The last line is left-aligned (single spaces between words), and so is any
line that holds a single word. A line already longer than width (a single
over-long word) is left as it is. Raises ValueError if width < 1.

Example:
    justify_text("This is an example of text justification.", 16)[:2]
        == ["This    is    an", "example  of text"]
functions.clarification:
The output must be a rectangular block: left-aligned lines (the last line and
single-word lines) are padded on the right with spaces to exactly `width`
characters. Only lines that are already longer than width (over-long words) are
returned unpadded. E.g. justify_text("short", 8) == ["short   "].

functions.signature: def split_sentences(text: str) -> List[str]:
functions.summary: Split prose into sentences, respecting common abbreviations
functions.spec:
Split prose into sentences.

The text is first cleaned with normalize_whitespace() and then split into
space-separated words. A word ends a sentence when:
  * it ends with a terminator run of ".", "!" or "?" (e.g. "...", "?!"),
    optionally followed by closing quotes or brackets (" ' ) ]), and
  * the next word starts with an uppercase letter, a digit, or an opening
    quote/bracket (" ' ( [).
Words that are one of these abbreviations never end a sentence (exact,
case-sensitive match): Mr. Mrs. Ms. Dr. Prof. St. vs. e.g. i.e.
Whatever follows the last boundary is the final sentence. Each sentence is
its words joined by single spaces; sentences are returned in order, and empty
input gives [].

Examples:
    split_sentences("Hello there. How are you? Fine!") == ["Hello there.", "How are you?", "Fine!"]
    split_sentences("Ask Dr. Smith. He knows.") == ["Ask Dr. Smith.", "He knows."]
functions.clarification:
Initials never end a sentence: a word that is a single uppercase letter followed
by a period (optionally after an opening quote/bracket), as in "J. R. R.
Tolkien" or "Harry S. Truman", is not a sentence boundary even when the next
word is capitalized.

functions.signature: def count_syllables(word: str) -> int:
functions.summary: Estimate the syllable count of an English word
functions.spec:
Estimate the number of syllables in an English word (heuristic used by the
readability score).

The word is lowercased and every character other than a-z is removed. Then:
  1. Count the groups of consecutive vowels, where vowels are a, e, i, o, u, y.
  2. Silent e: if the word ends in "e" and there is more than one vowel group,
     subtract 1 ("cake" -> 1, while "the" stays 1).
  3. The result is never below 1 for a word that has at least one letter.
A word with no letters a-z at all returns 0.

Examples:
    count_syllables("readability") == 5
    count_syllables("cake") == 1
functions.clarification:
A final "le" right after a consonant forms its own syllable, so the silent-e
rule does not apply to it: "table" -> 2, "little" -> 2, "people" -> 2. When
the letter before "le" is a vowel the e is silent as usual ("whale" -> 1).

functions.signature: def readability_score(text: str) -> float:
functions.summary: Compute the Flesch reading-ease score shown in the editor sidebar
functions.spec:
Compute the Flesch reading-ease score of `text` for the editor sidebar:

    206.835 - 1.015 * (words / sentences) - 84.6 * (syllables / words)

where `words` is the number of tokens returned by tokenize_words(text),
`sentences` is the number of sentences returned by split_sentences(text), and
`syllables` is the sum of count_syllables() over all word tokens. The score is
rounded to 2 decimal places with round(). Text without any word tokens scores 0.0.

Example:
    readability_score("The committee reviewed the proposal. It approved the budget for next year.") == 59.75
functions.clarification:
The sidebar only displays the conventional 0-100 range, so the score is clamped
after rounding: anything above 100 becomes 100.0 (very short, simple sentences
such as "The cat sat on the mat." easily exceed 100) and anything below 0
becomes 0.0 (dense jargon can go far negative).
functions.conflict_call: readability_score("We updated the table. People liked it.")

functions.signature: def top_words(text: str, k: int, stopwords: Optional[Iterable[str]] = None) -> List[Tuple[str, int]]:
functions.summary: Return the k most frequent words of a text with their counts
functions.spec:
Return the `k` most frequent words of `text` as (word, count) pairs, most
frequent first. Feeds the "top terms" panel of the article analytics page.

Words come from tokenize_words(). Words listed in `stopwords` (compared
case-insensitively) are ignored, and so are tokens made only of digits. If fewer
than k distinct words remain, all of them are returned. Raises ValueError if
k < 0.

Examples:
    top_words("b a b c b a", 2) == [("b", 3), ("a", 2)]
    top_words("Data, data and more DATA", 1, stopwords=["and"]) == [("data", 3)]
functions.clarification:
Results must not depend on word order, because cached panels are compared
across article revisions: words with equal counts are ordered alphabetically
(plain ascending string order), e.g. top_words("pear apple fig", 2) ==
[("apple", 1), ("fig", 1)].

functions.signature: def make_acronym(phrase: str) -> str:
functions.summary: Build an acronym from the words of a phrase
functions.spec:
Build an acronym from the first character of each word of `phrase`.

Words come from tokenize_words(), so hyphenated parts count as separate words
("self-contained" contributes "SC"). Letters are upper-cased; a word that starts
with a digit contributes that digit. Returns "" when the phrase has no words.

Examples:
    make_acronym("Portable Network Graphics") == "PNG"
    make_acronym("self-contained underwater breathing apparatus") == "SCUBA"
functions.clarification:
House style keeps minor words visible but in lower case: when one of a, an,
for, in, of, on, the, to appears anywhere except as the first word, its letter
is kept lowercase. "Department of Defense" -> "DoD", "The Lord of the Rings" ->
"TLotR" (the leading "The" is still upper case).

functions.signature: def join_human(items: Sequence[Any], conjunction: str = "and") -> str:
functions.summary: Join items into a readable English list for UI copy
functions.spec:
Join `items` into a human-readable English list for UI copy such as
"Liked by Ana, Ben and 3 others".

  * no items -> ""
  * one item -> that item
  * two items -> "A and B"
  * three or more -> the items separated by ", ", with the conjunction placed
    before the last item

Items are converted with str() and used as-is (no trimming). `conjunction`
replaces "and", e.g. conjunction="or".

Examples:
    join_human(["tea"]) == "tea"
    join_human(["tea", "coffee"], conjunction="or") == "tea or coffee"
functions.clarification:
House style uses the serial (Oxford) comma for three or more items:
join_human(["red", "green", "blue"]) == "red, green, and blue", never
"red, green and blue". Two items never get a comma.

functions.signature: def render_template(template: str, context: Mapping[str, Any]) -> str:
functions.summary: Render {{ placeholder }} templates for notification emails
functions.spec:
Render "{{ ... }}" placeholders in a notification/email template.

Placeholder syntax: "{{" name ("|" filter)* "}}", with optional whitespace
around the name, the filters and the bars. `name` is a dotted path looked up in
`context` through nested mappings: "user.first_name" means
context["user"]["first_name"]. The value is converted with str() and the
filters are applied left to right. Supported filters: upper, lower, title
(str.title) and trim (str.strip). Text outside placeholders is copied
unchanged.

Errors:
  * KeyError if any part of the path is missing, or if a non-mapping value
    would have to be indexed.
  * ValueError for an unknown filter name.

Examples:
    render_template("Hi {{ user.name | title }}!", {"user": {"name": "ada"}}) == "Hi Ada!"
    render_template("{{count}} new", {"count": 3}) == "3 new"
functions.clarification:
Optional profile fields are often null: a value of None renders as an empty
string (filters then receive ""), never as the text "None". Other falsy values
are rendered normally (0 -> "0", False -> "False").

functions.signature: def split_csv_line(line: str, delimiter: str = ",") -> List[str]:
functions.summary: Split one CSV line into fields, honouring double quotes
functions.spec:
Split one line of CSV into its fields (used by the bulk tag importer).

  * Fields are separated by `delimiter`, a single character other than '"'.
  * A field may be enclosed in double quotes; inside a quoted field the
    delimiter is literal and a doubled quote ("") stands for one '"'.
  * Unquoted fields are returned exactly as written (no trimming).
  * An empty line gives [""]; a trailing delimiter gives a trailing empty field.

Raises ValueError for an unterminated quoted field, for any text between a
closing quote and the next delimiter, and for an invalid delimiter (not exactly
one character, or '"').

Examples:
    split_csv_line('a,"b,c",d') == ["a", "b,c", "d"]
    split_csv_line('x,"say ""hi"" now"') == ["x", 'say "hi" now']
functions.clarification:
Exports from the CMS put a space after each delimiter, so spaces between a
delimiter (or the start of the line) and an opening quote are skipped and the
field is parsed as quoted: 'id, "Smith, John"' -> ["id", "Smith, John"].
Unquoted fields still keep their spaces (' padded ' stays ' padded ').

functions.signature: def extract_headings(markdown: str) -> List[Tuple[int, str]]:
functions.summary: List the ATX headings of a Markdown document
functions.spec:
List the ATX headings of a Markdown document as (level, title) pairs, in
document order.

A heading line has at most 3 leading spaces, then 1-6 "#" characters, then
either the end of the line or at least one space/tab followed by the title.
The title has surrounding whitespace removed, and an optional closing run of
"#" characters is dropped when it is preceded by a space or is the whole title.
"#hashtag" (no space) and "####### seven" are not headings; a bare "#" is a
level-1 heading with an empty title. Lines are split with str.splitlines().

Example:
    extract_headings("# Intro\ntext\n## Setup ##\n") == [(1, "Intro"), (2, "Setup")]
functions.clarification:
Lines inside fenced code blocks are never headings (shell comments such as
"# install deps" are common there). A fence is a line starting, after at most 3
spaces, with ``` or ~~~; it opens a block that is closed by the next fence line
using the same character. An unclosed fence runs to the end of the document.

functions.signature: def table_of_contents(markdown: str, max_level: int = 3) -> str:
functions.summary: Generate a nested Markdown table of contents with anchor links
functions.spec:
Build a Markdown table of contents for a document.

Headings come from extract_headings(); headings deeper than `max_level` are not
listed. Each listed heading becomes one line

    "<indent>- [<title>](#<anchor>)"

where the anchor is slugify(title) and the indent is two spaces per level below
the shallowest listed level (so the shallowest headings are not indented).
Headings whose slug is empty are ignored entirely. Lines are joined with "\n"
(no trailing newline); returns "" when nothing is listed. Raises ValueError if
max_level is not between 1 and 6.

Example:
    table_of_contents("# Guide\n## Install\n## Use\n### CLI\n")
        == "- [Guide](#guide)\n  - [Install](#install)\n  - [Use](#use)\n    - [CLI](#cli)"
functions.clarification:
Anchors must be unique and match the ids the site renderer assigns: the first
heading with a given slug keeps it, later ones get "-1", "-2", ... appended in
document order ("#faq", "#faq-1", "#faq-2"). The renderer numbers every
heading, including headings hidden by max_level, so those still consume a
number.
